To pine means to feel a deep, quiet, and lasting sadness because you want something — or someone — that you cannot have, or that is no longer with you. It is not just wanting something. It is wanting something so much that it hurts, and you feel somewhat helpless about it.

Think of it as a dull ache inside you that just doesn't go away.
What makes it different from just "wanting"

If you want a new phone, you don't pine for it. Pining is far more emotional and far more painful than ordinary wanting. It almost always involves a sense of loss, distance, or impossibility. You pine for things you had and lost, or things you deeply love but can't reach.

Also, pining is passive. The person pining is usually not doing much about it — they are just quietly suffering that longing. This is an important part of the word's character.
The typical situations where "pine" is used

For a person: This is the most common use. Someone loves another person who is gone, far away, or simply doesn't love them back — and they ache for them silently. "He had moved to another country, and she pined for him every single day."

For a place: People often pine for their homeland, their childhood home, or a place that gave them happiness. "Living in the city, he constantly pined for the quiet village he grew up in."

For a time: You can pine for the past — for a simpler, happier time in your life that you can never return to. "She pined for the carefree days of her youth."

For a thing or feeling: More broadly, you can pine for anything that once made you feel whole, safe, or happy. A sick person might pine for their health. A lonely person might pine for friendship.

When someone pines so deeply and for so long that they become visibly weak, sad, or withdrawn — wasting away emotionally (and sometimes physically) — we say they pine away. "After his wife passed, he just pined away, barely eating or speaking." This version of the word emphasises the slow, consuming nature of the grief.

The word carries a distinctly melancholic, tender quality. It's not loud grief. It's not angry frustration. It's a quiet, sustained ache — the kind of longing you carry around with you daily, not the kind that explodes. This is why it often appears in poetry, literature, and romantic contexts. It captures a very human emotional experience: wanting something beautiful that is simply out of reach.
How it sits among similar words

You yearn for something you strongly desire. You long for something you want deeply. You hanker for something, often casually. But when you pine, you don't just desire — you silently suffer that desire, with a sense of sadness and helplessness attached to it. Pine is the most emotionally heavy of these words.

You will almost always see "pine" followed by the word for or after:

  • Pine for someone/something — the standard, everyday form. "She pined for her old life."
  • Pine after someone — slightly old-fashioned, often used for romantic longing. "He pined after her for years."
  • Pine away — to waste away from longing or grief. "He pined away in her absence."
One sentence to remember it by
If you ever forget the word, come back to this image: a person sitting by a window, staring into the distance, silently aching for someone they love who is no longer there. That is pining.
